issue_context.title: Exception message for assert(0) depends on whitespace
issue_context.body:
<!--
Thank you for reporting a possible bug in Node.js.

Please fill in as much of the template below as you can.

Version: output of `node -v`
Platform: output of `uname -a` (UNIX), or version and 32 or 64-bit (Windows)
Subsystem: if known, please specify the affected core module name

If possible, please provide code that demonstrates the problem, keeping it as
simple and free of external dependencies as you can.
-->

* **Version**: 10, 12
* **Platform**: macOS High Sierra 10.13.6
* **Subsystem**: Assert

<!-- Please provide more details below this comment. -->
Under Node 10 and Node 12, generating an exception from an assertion failure returns a different assertion failure message depending on differences in whitespace. It seems that with a certain whitespace configuration we see the Node 8 assertion failure message `0 == true`, other configurations will generate the Node 10 message `The expression evaluated to a falsy value`.  This issue only seems to affect the exception message, all other behaviour seems consistent.

This will affect anything that runs minified source.

I have included a simple reproduction of the issue [here](https://github.com/AndrewFinlay/node_exception_example)
comments: @AndrewFinlay thank you for the report. This should indeed not fail to create the better error message.

@Himself65 @pd4d10 is correct about that. The start is set to zero to include `assert` or what ever name the user named it. It would otherwise only show `ok()`.

I am currently looking into it (there is an easy solution but that would waste a lot of CPU time, so I am trying to find a proper fix).

review_comments:
There are multiple cases that won't fit into this pattern. Think about e.g., the assertion being before the `try / catch`.

There are also probably more things that might cause failures, not just `try / catch`. I personally feel like this needs a deeper refactoring.

There is indeed one simple fix that will always work but that would cause CPU spikes in some cases, so I do not even propose it ;-).
I think there must be `try` keywords on the first line after reading the whole codes. Don't it?
Yes, but it could be behind the assertion. Think about e.g., minified code. I can not think of any regular expression that guarantees that things work as expected. We need an AST for it.
We already have a test case like the second one.
